title: Richard Tromans (Artificial Lawyer) — AL View: Claude For Legal Moves Centre Stage
author: Richard Tromans

dom.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: Tromans accepts that AI adoption is shaped by competitive positioning and operational integration, then materially extends the cluster by showing how a frontier-model provider can both supply and cannibalise legal-tech vendors. He also identifies individual customisation, technical support, privacy diligence and incumbent workflows as concrete constraints on adoption. He does not address the cluster’s pricing, staffing or buyer-power claims.
qs: > > Finally, it really is a strange scenario when a long line of legal tech companies are waiting to announce how they are now working with a business that is eating – or promises to eat – part of *their* business.
customisation here is great, but that means **taking the time and delivering the tech assistance to each lawyer to make that real, accurate and reliable**.

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: Tromans accepts that Anthropic is moving into the centre of legal workflows and becoming both supplier and competitor to specialist vendors. He materially develops the proposition by identifying complementary vendor roles, implementation and service-capacity constraints, business-model differences between firms and in-house teams, and renewal cycles as the likely point at which displacement pressure becomes concrete.
qs: > > As AL said in this week's earlier article, **Claude for Legal becomes the legal AI fabric**, the legal tech companies embroider in their curated data and specialist workflows (at least for now), and then all of this is woven through MS Word and Excel.

> **The real challenge will probably be in two or three years**, when Claude for Legal is deeply embedded in how many lawyers work, spend there will have gone up, and at the same time many legal tech point solutions will be facing renewals.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Tromans accepts that value comes from embedding AI into tailored workflows rather than merely procuring a powerful model. He materially extends the cluster with a platform-specific account of Microsoft 365 integration and lawyer-level customisation, while identifying technical support, privacy review, incumbent workflows and firm-wide scaling as practical constraints. His claims are mainly implementation analysis and market prediction, not evidence of general legal competence or realised organisation-wide value.
qs: customisation here is great, but that means **taking the time and delivering the tech assistance to each lawyer to make that real, accurate and reliable**.
And doing that in a firm of several hundred lawyers, or even a few thousands, across many countries, will not be easy at all or quick.

st.t: Workflow control: Foundation models challenge specialist interfaces
st.an: Tromans accepts the cluster’s central claim that foundation-model companies are moving into lawyers’ daily workflows and materially develops it by identifying customisation and Microsoft integration as routes to interface control. He also specifies the resulting supplier-partner tension, implementation constraints and likely renewal pressure on point solutions, while treating displacement and consolidation as conditional forecasts rather than established outcomes.
qs: > > As AL said in this week's earlier article, **Claude for Legal becomes the legal AI fabric**, the legal tech companies embroider in their curated data and specialist workflows (at least for now), and then all of this is woven through MS Word and Excel.

> **The real challenge will probably be in two or three years**, when Claude for Legal is deeply embedded in how many lawyers work, spend there will have gone up, and at the same time many legal tech point solutions will be facing renewals.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: Tromans supports the cluster’s central platform thesis: customisation and integrations could make Claude the primary layer for legal work and pressure specialist software. He also supports the qualification that displacement is not established, identifying specialist legal data, incumbent workflows, privacy checks and implementation burdens as continuing protections and constraints.
qs: > > As AL said in this week's earlier article, **Claude for Legal becomes the legal AI fabric**, the legal tech companies embroider in their curated data and specialist workflows (at least for now), and then all of this is woven through MS Word and Excel.

> **What You Can Do Now, And Where This Is Headed** > > Pike outlined what is possible today, such as the 12 legal plugins (see below) and the MCP connectors to a host of legal tech companies, including Thomson Reuters – which is very excited about how this helps them, given that they are a legal data giant and Anthropic cannot replace them – at least on this aspect.

kp.k: Anthropic seeks a central position in legal workflows
kp.d: Tromans interprets Anthropic's webinar as evidence of a deliberate legal-market expansion rather than a supporting role for existing software vendors. He reports growth from 1 to 12 legal plugins in a few months, with Claude Cowork and Microsoft application integrations central to the offering. His account of competitive intent is an interpretation of the presentation, not a measured market-share finding.
qs: It's very clear: Claude wants to be very much inside lawyers' workflows. This is not a side project.
it's gone from 1 to 12 legal plugins in a few months
Ultimately, Anthropic is a tech company that is seeking to take market share – as well as aspiring to change the world for the better.

kp.k: Enterprise legal demand supports Anthropic's commercial expansion
kp.d: Tromans links Anthropic's legal strategy to its asserted IPO ambitions, revenue needs, addressable market and demand for heavy business users. He portrays document-intensive legal enterprise work and rapidly growing lawyer interest as commercially attractive, but supplies no usage, revenue or adoption measurements.
qs: Anthropic is heading towards one of the largest IPOs ever.
It needs heavy users – and its business-user pool is growing.
Legal enterprise, with its millions and millions of documents, and its relentless needs, fits very nicely into this AI engagement trajectory.

kp.k: Process automation exposes differences between legal business models
kp.d: Tromans reports Pike's augmentation narrative: Claude absorbs process work so lawyers can provide higher-value input. He contrasts this with traditional firms earning substantial income from unautomated process work, while describing in-house teams and NewMod Crosby as facing less business-model friction. Pike relayed Crosby CEO Ryan Daniels's workflow-agent claim; Crosby, Freshfields and Accenture were the three organisations on the customer slide, not a systematic adoption sample.
qs: Pike stayed with the general narrative that Claude is there to soak up process work, which then allows lawyers to handle more value-added input.
He didn't dwell on the reality that many law firms make a significant chunk of their income from *not* automating process work.
inhouse teams have far less process friction here than law firms.
a comment by CEO, **Ryan Daniels**, about putting Claude 'agents' into their workflows so they can focus on higher value work.

kp.k: Due diligence software faces emerging frontier-model competition
kp.d: An M&A plugin demonstration showed tabular review. Tromans acknowledges that the workflow may not yet be smooth, but judges it a potentially formidable competitor to SaaS products primarily selling AI-driven due diligence. This is a face-value assessment of a demonstration, not comparative testing of accuracy or performance.
qs: There was a demo of one part of one of the plugins, for M&A, and they showed off how tabular review works.

it may not be the smoothest workflow yet, but on face value AL would say that if you make money from selling a SaaS product primarily based on AI-driven due diligence then you have a very formidable competitor all of a sudden.

kp.k: Customisation makes lawyers builders and embeds AI in work
kp.d: The webinar presented lawyers becoming builders as professional evolution. Tromans distinguishes dialogue that supplies business context from editing plugins' natural-language instructions. He argues that tailoring increases usefulness and makes Claude intertwined with daily work, positioning it as underlying infrastructure across Word and Excel while vendors contribute curated data and specialist workflows.
qs: That lawyers becoming 'builders' is just a natural progression and part of how the profession is evolving,
You can tweak the vanilla plugins – which in a non-technical way are simply a bunch of instructions in natural language

With customisation comes two things: first you can make Claude for Legal way more useful for your needs, and thus push up value creation; and second, **it will become symbiotic with your daily work**, because you've tailored it to address your specific needs.

kp.k: Practice-area expansion remains an ongoing vendor ambition
kp.d: Pike described incremental expansion of the plugin taxonomy, naming environmental and tax law, and reported enthusiasm from eDiscovery users. Tromans treats these statements as indications that expansion will continue; they are prospective vendor statements rather than evidence that those additional capabilities have been delivered.
qs: There will be incremental progress along the way.
environmental law, tax law
People in eDiscovery are excited about Claude.
In short, this is not about to pause. This is the beginning.

kp.k: Individual customisation requires technical assistance and implementation time
kp.d: Despite natural-language operation, Tromans says meaningful modification through GitHub markdowns requires technical familiarity or assistance. Firms and in-house teams may obtain internal help or consultants. Citing Greg Lambert's emphasis on individual lawyer needs, he warns that reliable, lawyer-specific implementation across hundreds or thousands of lawyers and multiple countries will be neither easy nor quick. A smoother future customisation experience is explicitly his guess.
qs: unless you are familiar with this type of environment then you will need some technical help to really achieve your goals.
AL would guess that eventually the whole customisation experience will become smoother.
taking the time and delivering the tech assistance to each lawyer to make that real, accurate and reliable
And doing that in a firm of several hundred lawyers, or even a few thousands, across many countries, will not be easy at all or quick.

kp.k: Duplicated spending may precede later software budget consolidation
kp.d: Tromans expects firms initially to retain data providers and most existing legal AI tools despite overlap. Token consumption and enterprise licences mean Claude is not necessarily cheap. He identifies a conditional challenge in two or three years: deeper embedding and increased Claude spending could coincide with point-solution renewals, prompting CTOs to consider budget cuts. He does not establish that cuts or net savings will occur.
qs: all law firms will keep their data providers and most will keep the legal AI tools they already have, **even if there is duplication here**.
token costs will mount up and you still need an enterprise Claude licence for everyone in the firm / team.

**The real challenge will probably be in two or three years**, when Claude for Legal is deeply embedded in how many lawyers work, spend there will have gone up, and at the same time many legal tech point solutions will be facing renewals.

kp.k: Dedicated implementation support remains an incumbent vendor advantage
kp.d: Tromans contrasts specialist vendors' accessible support with Claude for Legal's lack of a large dedicated sales and services team. He argues that Anthropic needs a much larger legal go-to-market and forward-deployed engineering operation. Expansion could particularly affect in-house teams lacking their own legal technology groups; without it, he considers Claude's growth trajectory less clear.
qs: Claude for Legal **does not have a massive dedicated sales and services team**.
Claude for Legal will need to build a far larger GTM / forward deployed engineering team for legal in the months and years to come.
If it does, then that could have a major impact, especially on the inhouse side where most teams won't have a legal tech group of their own.
If it doesn't, then the growth trajectory of Claude for Legal is less clear.

kp.k: Vendor accommodation combines complementarity with cannibalisation risk
kp.d: Tromans describes legal technology companies connecting to Claude while hoping their data and specialist workflows remain sufficiently differentiated. He identifies Thomson Reuters's legal data as a complementary asset Anthropic cannot replace in that respect. He reports vendors' hopes that Anthropic's reach will expand overall demand despite cannibalisation, and agrees there is a current awareness benefit; eventual net gains remain uncertain.
qs: including Thomson Reuters – which is very excited about how this helps them, given that they are a legal data giant and Anthropic cannot replace them – at least on this aspect.
they hope what they offer is unique and moated enough to survive the engagement.
An indirect benefit is more interest in today's incumbent legal AI tools.
**They also hope that such a massive player will actually drive up demand for legal AI tools overall, and despite some cannibalisation, that there is a net gain from all of this.**

kp.k: Privacy checks and established workflows constrain displacement
kp.d: Although Pike addressed privacy and offered assurances, Tromans says firms and in-house teams must undertake their own checks. Existing relationships and workflows also make switching uncertain: overlapping functionality does not establish that lawyers will abandon incumbent tools for plugins.
qs: Then you have all the privacy aspects, which Pike addressed head on and assured people. Although, all firms and inhouse teams will have to do those checks to reassure themselves.
And then you have all the incumbent relationships and workflows that lawyers use today.
It's not a slam dunk that they will abandon those for a plugin.

kp.k: Further restructuring and frontier-model entry remain speculative
kp.d: Tromans raises possible industry consolidation and software companies becoming NewMods rather than continuing to sell software, without presenting these as established developments. He also reports unnamed-source information that another major AI company is preparing a substantial legal push and has made key hires, while explicitly acknowledging that its form is unknown.
qs: Maybe we will see more consolidation, and maybe some legal tech companies will turn into NewMods and stop trying to sell software in this new environment? We shall see.
AL has on good authority that another major AI player is preparing to go large in legal.
How that will manifest itself is not known yet, but it's understood that key hires have taken place already.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Tromans predicts that Claude for Legal will become a central legal-work platform, expand across practice areas, and both compete with and complement specialist legal-tech suppliers.
pts.d: Tromans interprets Anthropic's webinar as demonstrating an intention to occupy lawyers' workflows rather than merely direct customers to other software suppliers. He presents customisable plugins and Microsoft Office integration as a basis for deeper everyday adoption. He reports Pike's account of Claude absorbing process work so lawyers can concentrate on higher-value input, while arguing that this conflicts with traditional firms' income from unautomated process work. Tromans sees the M&A tabular-review demonstration as evidence of emerging competition for AI due-diligence software. He predicts more lawyer adoption and wider practice coverage, but treats consolidation and vendors becoming NewMod legal-service businesses as possibilities rather than settled outcomes. He also records the countervailing possibility that Anthropic's reach expands demand for incumbent legal-AI products enough to offset cannibalisation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is a product webinar, a demonstration, reported customer examples, Tromans's observations and market reasoning, and an unnamed source—not measured productivity or market-impact results.
pts.d: Tromans bases his platform-expansion interpretation on the webinar's emphasis on plugins, customisation, Cowork and Office integration, and reports growth from one to twelve plugins over a few months. The M&A demonstration supports his competitive assessment, expressly qualified as a face-value impression of a workflow that may not yet be smooth. Customer references include Crosby, Freshfields and Accenture; the account of Crosby using agents for higher-value work is a reported customer example, not an independently measured outcome. His assessment of implementation difficulty draws on examining GitHub environments and the plugin customisation process. His revenue and market-share interpretation also invokes Anthropic's anticipated IPO, demand for heavy business users, and legal enterprise's document volumes, without quantitative supporting analysis. The closing prediction of another major AI entrant relies on unnamed authority and reported hires. The article supplies no benchmarks, quantified savings, controlled comparisons or measured adoption rates.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Tromans distinguishes current availability and complementary adoption from a possible budget reckoning in two or three years; expansion depends on implementation support, privacy checks and displacement of established workflows.
pts.d: Writing in May 2026, Tromans describes twelve plugins and Office integration as current offerings and anticipates continued expansion. He reports Pike's statement that progress will be incremental, with environmental and tax law among possible future areas. In the near term, Tromans expects firms to retain data providers and most existing legal-AI tools despite duplication; he does not establish that Claude will reduce total spending, noting token costs and enterprise licences. He places the likely competitive budget challenge two or three years ahead, when embedded Claude usage and higher spending coincide with point-solution renewals, framing budget trimming as a question. Wider growth depends on Anthropic building legal sales and services capacity in the coming months and years. Individual customisation requires time and technical help, particularly at multinational-firm scale. Privacy reviews and incumbent relationships further qualify adoption. Smoother future customisation is explicitly his guess, and the form and timing of the other reported major AI entrant remain unspecified.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects differ across traditional firms, in-house teams, NewMod service providers, specialist software vendors, data suppliers and individual lawyers.
pts.d: For individual lawyers, Tromans envisages a customisable AI companion embedded in familiar Office applications and a growing role in building their own tools. Traditional firms face tension between process automation and existing fee income, plus implementation and licensing costs; their CTOs may later choose among overlapping products. In-house legal teams face less of that revenue-model friction, but many lack internal legal-tech teams and therefore depend on external support. Tromans portrays NewMod businesses such as Crosby as particularly able to use Claude at scale without the same business-model conflict. Specialist SaaS vendors, especially AI due-diligence suppliers, face substitution risk while retaining opportunities to supply curated data, specialist workflows and customer service. He presents Thomson Reuters' legal-data role as less replaceable on that particular dimension. Vendors may also gain from increased market awareness, while some could shift from selling software to delivering legal services. The article does not make a specific access-to-justice claim or quantify lawyer employment effects.
